newsitem.title: USA: Judge strikes down Alabama school prayer law.
newsitem.headline: Judge strikes down Alabama school prayer law.

text.p: A federal judge Thursday struck down an Alabama law that had allowed prayer in the state's public school systems since 1993.

U.S. District Judge Ira DeMent, ruling on a challenge filed more than a year ago by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), concluded that the law endorsed religion and entangled the government in religious activity, thus violating the separation of church and state set forth in the Constitution.
Attorneys for the state of Alabama threatened to fight the ruling all the way to the U.S. Supreme Court.

"It's totally up in the air right now and the Supreme Court is going to have to come in and say something," said lawyer A. Eric Johnston, who represented Alabama's Republican Gov. Fob James, a staunch advocate of prayer in school.
The Alabama law, passed by the state Legislature in 1993, condoned prayers that were non-sectarian, non-proselytising and student-initiated.
The ACLU sued the state and two county school boards in February 1996, claiming the law created a favoured place for prayer in school and singled out religious speech for special treatment.

An assistant principal from Dekalb County, Alabama, who joined the ACLU complaint, charged that school officials allowed prayers to be read over a public address system at football games and required attendance at an assembly on AIDS and drug abuse led by a Christian evangelist who peppered his speech with Biblical readings.
Meanwhile, state officials were reviewing the ruling to determine what effect it could have on a proposal to combine mandatory prayer with school civic lessons.
The Alabama Legislature also has been considering a measure to allow the Ten Commandments to be displayed in state courtrooms.
